c.tagline: Sun-drenched Algarve gateway of a walled old town and the Ria Formosa lagoon.

taxi.fareNote: Metered fares with surcharges at night, on weekends and from the airport, plus a small luggage fee; short trips have a minimum charge.

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide emergency number reaching police, fire and ambulance, with English-speaking operators.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_desc: The walled medieval old town entered through the Arco da Vila, a cluster of cobbled lanes around the cathedral, bishop's palace and bone chapel; Faro's most atmospheric, sightseeing-rich quarter.

The lively pedestrian downtown between the marina and the Manuel Bivar garden, packed with shops, cafes, restaurants and nightlife along Rua de Santo António; the convenient central base for most visitors.
The city's long Atlantic sand beach on the Ancão peninsula at the edge of the Ria Formosa, a strip of beach bars and seafood restaurants; relaxed and summery but a short drive or bus from town.
A quiet residential parish just west of the centre near the airport and university, with local eateries and easy airport access; practical and calm rather than touristy.
A modern residential district on the eastern edge of the city with its own small train halt and everyday amenities; an affordable, local-feeling place to stay near the centre.

water.note: Tap water is safe, though some prefer bottled for taste.

transit.hours: City buses run roughly 7:00 AM to 9:00 PM with reduced weekend service; trains run through the day into the evening.
transit.note: Faro has no metro or tram. Próximo and ViaFaro city buses serve the town, airport and beach, while Comboios de Portugal (CP) trains link Faro along the Algarve line and north to Lisbon and Porto.
transit.pay: Bus fares are paid in cash to the driver or with a rechargeable card; train tickets are bought at station machines, the ticket office or the CP app.

ferry: Ria Formosa ferries to Ilha Deserta, Farol & Culatra (Portas do Mar)
train: Faro railway station (CP — Alfa Pendular, Intercidades, Regional)

transit.m: Próximo bus line 14 or 16 to the bus terminal/centre, ~20 min
Taxi to the city centre, ~10-15 min

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up or leaving ~5-10% for good service in restaurants is appreciated.

food.name: Cataplana de marisco
food.desc: Clams, prawns, fish and chourico steamed in a hinged copper cataplana with tomato, pepper and coriander. Usually a minimum order for two.

places.name: Tertulia Algarvia
places.note: Regional-cuisine specialist inside the walls; cataplana and Algarve classics done traditionally.

places.name: Faz Gostos
places.note: Long-established fine-dining Algarvian kitchen; the cataplana is a signature, best booked ahead.

places.name: Vila Adentro
places.note: Tiled courtyard restaurant inside the old walls with regional seafood and a strong wine list.

food.name: Xarem com conquilhas
food.desc: Soupy Algarve cornmeal porridge stirred with wedge clams, garlic, olive oil and coriander. Fishing-village comfort food from the Ria Formosa.

places.name: Tertulia Algarvia
places.note: One of the few central kitchens that keeps xarem on the menu year round.

places.name: A Venda
places.note: Small, well-reviewed petiscos house doing rustic Algarve dishes with local produce.

places.name: Ria Formosa waterfront restaurants
places.note: Harbour-side kitchens serve xarem best in spring and summer when clams are freshest.

food.name: Conquilhas a Algarvia
food.desc: Tiny sweet wedge clams from the Ria Formosa sand flats, flash-cooked with garlic, olive oil, white wine and coriander. Eat with bread for the juices.

places.name: Mercado Municipal de Faro
places.note: Buy them at the fish hall or eat at the market cafes; freshest and cheapest option.

places.name: A Venda
places.note: Petiscos-style plates of clams and shellfish in a relaxed neighbourhood room.

places.name: Vila Adentro
places.note: Clams served as a starter before the cataplana; good setting inside the city walls.

food.name: Arroz de marisco and arroz de lingueirao
food.desc: Loose, brothy seafood rice, made in Faro with razor clams, prawns or cockles, tomato and plenty of coriander. Served in the pan.

places.name: Faz Gostos
places.note: Careful, generous seafood rice from a kitchen that has anchored Faro dining for years.

places.name: Ria Formosa waterfront restaurants
places.note: Marina-side dining rooms that cook rice dishes to order with the day's shellfish.

places.name: Tertulia Algarvia
places.note: Regional menu that pairs seafood rice with Algarve wines by the glass.

food.name: Grilled fish and sardines
food.desc: Sea bream, sea bass, sardines and horse mackerel salted and grilled over charcoal, served with boiled potatoes and a simple tomato salad.

places.name: Chefe Branco
places.note: Popular grill house locals use for straightforward charcoal-cooked fish at fair prices.

places.name: Mercado Municipal de Faro
places.note: Pick your fish downstairs, eat it grilled upstairs; best value seafood lunch in the city.

places.name: Ilha do Farol and Culatra beach shacks
places.note: Short ferry from Faro to island grills serving whatever the boats landed that morning.

food.name: Dom Rodrigo and Algarve almond sweets
food.desc: Foil-wrapped twists of fios de ovos, egg yolk, almond, sugar and cinnamon, plus marzipan figs and morgado. Convent sweets of the Algarve.

places.name: Pastelaria Gardy
places.note: Faro's best-known cake shop, going for decades; regional sweets and good pasteis de nata.

places.name: Casa Algarvia
places.note: Regional produce shop selling Dom Rodrigo, fig and almond sweets to take home.

places.name: Mercado Municipal de Faro
places.note: Stalls sell boxed convent sweets and dried figs alongside the fish and produce.

food.name: Medronho
food.desc: Fierce clear spirit distilled from arbutus berries in the Monchique hills, drunk as a digestif or splashed into coffee as cafe com cheirinho.

places.name: Bar Columbus
places.note: Landmark arcaded bar on the marina garden; easy place to try medronho and local spirits.

places.name: Casa Algarvia
places.note: Sells bottled artisan medronho and honey-sweetened melosa from small Monchique producers.

places.name: Old town tascas
places.note: Small local bars inside the walls pour medronho by the shot after a meal.

food.name: Algarve wine
food.desc: Warm-climate whites from Lagoa and Tavira DOC plus Negra Mole reds, increasingly good and rarely exported, so drink them here.

places.name: Vila Adentro
places.note: Old-walls restaurant with an Algarve-focused list and staff who will talk you through it.

places.name: Faz Gostos
places.note: Broad Portuguese cellar with a solid regional section for pairing with cataplana.

places.name: Bar Columbus
places.note: Central terrace bar for a glass of Algarve white while watching the marina.

landmarks: Cidade Velha (Old Town) and Arco da Vila
Faro's storybook walled quarter, entered through a neoclassical arch where storks nest atop an 11th-century Moorish horseshoe gate.
Faro Cathedral (Sé de Faro)
A 13th-century cathedral blending Gothic, Renaissance and baroque styles, with a bone chapel and a bell-tower panorama over the lagoon.
Igreja do Carmo and Capela dos Ossos
A gilded baroque church concealing a macabre chapel lined with the skulls and bones of more than a thousand monks.
Ria Formosa Natural Park
A shimmering maze of lagoons, barrier islands and salt pans stretching 60 kilometers, sheltering flamingos, seahorses and clam harvesters.
Ilha Deserta (Barreta Island)
An uninhabited barrier island of pristine dunes and empty Atlantic sand at Portugal's southernmost point, reached by ferry from Faro's pier.
Ilha de Faro (Praia de Faro)
The city's own beach island, a long sandbar of golden strand, seafood shacks and lagoon-side calm minutes from the airport.
Museu Municipal de Faro
Housed in a 16th-century convent with a serene two-story cloister, displaying a remarkable Roman mosaic of Oceanus unearthed nearby.
Jardim Manuel Bivar
The palm-shaded marina garden at the old town's doorstep, where cafe terraces overlook bobbing boats and the Ria Formosa beyond.
Palácio de Estoi
A flamboyant rococo-revival palace in a nearby village, its pink facades, azulejo terraces and formal gardens now fronting a pousada hotel.
Milreu Roman Ruins
The remains of a luxurious Roman villa near Estoi, with fish-themed mosaics and a temple later converted into an early Christian church.

train.note: Faro station is the Algarve rail hub: the Alfa Pendular and Intercidades run north to Lisbon (~3h) and on to Porto, while CP Regional trains run east-west across the Algarve to Lagos and Vila Real de Santo António. There is no rail link to Spain.

bus.note: Rede Expressos and FlixBus run long-distance coaches to Lisbon and across Portugal; FlixBus and DAMAS cross into Andalusia (Seville, Huelva), roughly 2 hours away.

intl.to: Ilha Deserta / Barreta (Portugal) - from Portas do Mar
Farol & Culatra (Portugal) - from the commercial wharf
intl.op: Faro municipal lagoon ferries — tickets at the wharf kiosk

ferry.note: Ferries and boat taxis from Portas do Mar and the commercial wharf serve the Ria Formosa barrier islands — Ilha Deserta (Barreta), Farol and Culatra; all are domestic lagoon routes.

half.name: Tavira
half.blurb: An elegant riverside town of churches, a Roman bridge and quiet island beaches (~40 min by train).

half.name: Olhão
half.blurb: A working fishing town with a famous seafood market and ferries to the Ria Formosa islands (~15 min).

half.name: Loulé
half.blurb: A Moorish-walled market town with a Saturday market and gypsum caves inland from the coast.

full.name: Lagos
full.blurb: A historic port in the western Algarve beside the dramatic golden cliffs of Ponta da Piedade (~1h40).

full.name: Seville
full.blurb: The Andalusian capital of flamenco, the Alcázar and a vast Gothic cathedral, just across the border (~2h).

full.name: Sagres & Cape St. Vincent
full.blurb: The rugged south-western tip of Europe, with a clifftop fortress and lighthouse (~2h).

full.name: Silves
full.blurb: The former Moorish capital of the Algarve, crowned by a red-sandstone castle (~1h).
